propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act challenging an RPD decision.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act] challenging a decision of a Refugee Protection Division member [RPD or the Member] rejecting the Applicant’s claim and concluding that he is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application challenging an RPD decision rejecting the applicant's refugee claim.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant was born in Palestine and holds a passport issued by the Palestine Authority.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was in born in Palestine and has a passport issued by the Palestine Authority.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant was born in Palestine and has a Palestinian passport.

propositions.text: In 1993, the Applicant and his family were sponsored to the United States where he became a permanent resident.
propositions.quote: In 1993, the Applicant was sponsored with his family to the United States and became a permanent resident of that country.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant became a US permanent resident in 1993 through family sponsorship.

propositions.text: The Applicant was convicted of theft in 1999, possession of a firearm in 2003 and 2009, and driving under the influence in 2005.
propositions.quote: In June 1999, the Applicant was convicted of theft; in June 2003, convicted of possession of a firearm; in December 2005, convicted of driving under the influence; and in December 2009, convicted again of possession of a firearm.

paragraphs.summary: The court lists the applicant's criminal convictions from 1999 to 2009.

propositions.text: In 2011, the Applicant was deported from the US to Jordan due to his criminality and stayed there for 3 months.
propositions.quote: In 2011, as a result of his criminality, the Applicant was deported from the United States to Jordan, where he remained for 3 months.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant was deported from the US to Jordan in 2011 and stayed there three months.

propositions.text: The Applicant left Jordan, sought entry to Canada via Montreal airport without claiming refugee protection, was denied entry and removed to Jordan, then sent to the West Bank for 10 days before seeking re-entry.
propositions.quote: At this point, the Applicant left Jordan and sought entry to Canada via the Montreal airport, where he did not seek refugee protection. He was denied entry and immediately removed to Jordan. Upon his return to Jordan, the authorities sent the Applicant to the West Bank, where he remained for 10 days prior to seeking re-entry into Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the applicant's denied entry to Canada via Montreal and subsequent removal to Jordan and the West Bank.

propositions.text: On June 26, 2012, the Applicant entered Canada via Toronto airport with a Palestinian passport and was immediately detained.
propositions.quote: On June 26, 2012, the Applicant entered Canada via the Toronto airport with a Palestinian passport. He was immediately detained.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant entered Canada in 2012 via Toronto and was detained immediately.

propositions.text: The Applicant's personal information form was filed with the RPD on July 26, 2012.
propositions.quote: On July 26, 2012, the Applicant’s personal information form [PIF] was filed with the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the applicant's personal information form was filed with the RPD in July 2012.

propositions.text: In August 2012, the Applicant retained Mr. Prescod, an ICCRC-licensed immigration consultant, to represent him.
propositions.quote: In August 2012, the Applicant retained Mr. Prescod, an immigration consultant licensed with the Immigration Consultants of Canada Regulatory Council [ICCRC], to represent him in his immigration matters.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant retained an ICCRC-licensed immigration consultant in August 2012.

propositions.text: On September 11, 2015, the Applicant attended his hearing represented by Mr. Prescod, and the Member issued a verbal decision refusing the refugee claim.
propositions.quote: On September 11, 2015, the Applicant, represented by Mr. Prescod, attended his hearing at which point the Member issued a verbal decision refusing the Applicant’s refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant's hearing occurred in 2015 and the refugee claim was refused verbally.

propositions.text: On November 13, 2015, the Applicant's current counsel requested a response from Mr. Prescod regarding concerns about the quality of representation.
propositions.quote: On November 13, 2015, the Applicant’s current counsel sent Mr. Prescod a request for response to concerns that the Applicant’s dealings with Mr. Prescod’s office raised serious concerns as to the quality of the representation provided to the Applicant for his refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the applicant's current counsel requested a response from Mr. Prescod about representation quality concerns.

propositions.text: On November 19, 2015, the Applicant's counsel filed a formal complaint against Mr. Prescod with the ICCRC.
propositions.quote: On November 19, 2015, the Applicant’s counsel, on behalf of the Applicant, filed a formal complaint against Mr. Prescod with the ICCRC.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a formal complaint was filed against Mr. Prescod with the ICCRC in November 2015.

propositions.text: The Member found the Applicant not credible due to implausibility, lack of detail, and absence of documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Member found that the Applicant was not a credible witness primarily due to the implausibility and the paucity of details of the described events, and that the Applicant lacked documentary evidence establishing the alleged country condition or corroborating the alleged events.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant not credible due to implausibility, lack of detail, and no documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Whether the Applicant was denied procedural fairness due to his immigration consultant’s alleged professional negligence.
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises the sole issue as to whether he was denied procedural fairness in his refugee claim as a result of his immigration consultant’s alleged professional negligence.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant raises the issue of denial of procedural fairness due to alleged negligence by his immigration consultant.

propositions.text: The standard of review for alleged denial of justice due to professional negligence is correctness, citing Khosa and Memari.
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review in a case of alleged denial of justice due to professional negligence is one of correctness: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43; Memari v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1196 at paras 30, 32 [Memari].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is correctness for alleged denial of justice due to professional negligence.

propositions.text: Applicant must prove counsel's incompetence caused breach of procedural fairness by meeting a three-part test.
propositions.quote: It is trite law that the Applicant has the onus of demonstrating that his counsel’s incompetence resulted in a breach of procedural fairness. In doing so, the Applicant must establish that all three prongs of the following tripartite test are met: 1. The representative's alleged acts or omissions constituted incompetence; 2. There was a miscarriage of justice in the sense that, but for the alleged conduct, there is a reasonable probability that the result of the original hearing would have been different; and 3. The representative be given notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the three-part test the applicant must meet to prove counsel's incompetence caused procedural unfairness.

propositions.text: The third criterion of notice and opportunity to respond is conceded by the Respondent and evidenced on file.
propositions.quote: The third criterion will not be address as the Respondent concedes its fulfilment and the evidence on file demonstrate that the necessary notice was provided.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the third criterion is conceded by the respondent and supported by evidence.

propositions.text: The complaint about counsel's performance must be clear and precise, citing Brown v Canada.
propositions.quote: With regard to the first criterion, the performance component, the complaint must be “clear and precise” (Brown v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1305 at para 64).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the complaint about counsel's performance must be clear and precise.

propositions.text: Mr. Prescod was negligent and incompetent, inadequately preparing the Applicant for the hearing.
propositions.quote: In this regard, the Applicant submits that Mr. Prescod’s actions and omissions amount to negligent and incompetent conduct. In support of this claim, the Applicant submits that Mr. Prescod did not adequately prepare him for his hearing;

propositions.text: The Applicant met only twice with Mr. Prescod’s associate for about 25 minutes each, whose legal training is unclear.
propositions.quote: instead the Applicant met with Mr. Prescod’s associate twice for approximately 25 minutes each time, and it is unclear whether this individual had any legal training.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges Mr. Prescod was negligent, inadequately preparing him and relying on an associate with unclear legal training.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges he raised concerns about PIF narrative quality with Mr. Prescod and was reassured about revisions by the IRB.
propositions.quote: the Applicant alleges he was reassured that if his PIF needed revision, the Immigration and Refugee Board would inform Mr. Prescod of this

propositions.text: Applicant maintains Mr. Prescod advised no need for additional documents as his office would submit them.
propositions.quote: Mr. Prescod advised him that he did not need to provide additional documents as Mr. Prescod’s office would submit the necessary documentation

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges he raised concerns about PIF narrative quality and was reassured by Mr. Prescod about revisions and document submissions.

propositions.text: Applicant's complaint about Mr. Prescod's representation is difficult to determine due to conflicting statements about documentation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s complaint regarding Mr. Prescod’s representation of the Applicant is difficult to determine

propositions.text: Applicant's claim that Mr. Prescod found no documentation is accurate per country condition materials but differs from what was told to hearing officer.
propositions.quote: which is not what he advised the hearing officer, but which appears to be an accurate statement of the absence of such documentation in the country condition materials

propositions.text: Court will not decide this issue as application must be rejected based on second criterion of the test.
propositions.quote: I am not required to decide that issue as I conclude that the application must be rejected based on the second criterion of the test

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant's complaint about Mr. Prescod's representation unclear but will reject application on second criterion without deciding issue.

propositions.text: Prejudice must manifest as procedural unfairness, compromised trial reliability, or another apparent form.
propositions.quote: the prejudice “must be manifested in procedural unfairness, the reliability of the trial result having been compromised, or another readily apparent form.”

paragraphs.summary: Justice Crampton stated prejudice must manifest as procedural unfairness or compromised trial reliability.

propositions.text: Applicant submits reasonable probability that Mr. Prescod's incompetence affected hearing outcome due to lack of documents.
propositions.quote: there is a reasonable probability that had it not been for Mr. Prescod’s alleged incompetence, the result of the original hearing would have been different

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Mr. Prescod's incompetence likely changed hearing outcome due to missing documents.

propositions.text: Court disagrees that additional documents would have changed outcome; evidence does not establish objective risk or undermine decision confidence.
propositions.quote: The additional evidence submitted in the record before this Court does not establish an objective risk and thus would not undermine the confidence in the outcome of the Member’s decision

paragraphs.summary: Court finds additional evidence insufficient to change hearing outcome or undermine decision confidence.

propositions.text: Applicant submits document supports claim of Hamas forced recruitment.
propositions.quote: the document titled Recruiting and building rockets, Hamas determined to retain Gaza grip dated October 15, 2014, supports his claims that “Hamas is turning towards increasing dubious means to secure support including forced recruitment.”

propositions.text: Document actually discusses Hamas financial difficulty and does not mention forced recruitment.
propositions.quote: However, the document speaks to Hamas’ financial difficulty and makes no reference whatsoever to forced recruitment

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claims document supports forced recruitment by Hamas; court finds document only discusses financial difficulty, no forced recruitment.

propositions.text: Applicant relies on Turkish news article claiming Hamas launched fresh recruitment drive in Gaza.
propositions.quote: Applicant also relies on a Turkish News agency article to support his claim that “Hamas has launched a fresh recruitment drive in the Gaza strip.”

propositions.text: Article describes recruitment as voluntary enlistment via flyers, not forced recruitment.
propositions.quote: The recruitment campaign referenced in the article describes enlistment as a voluntary process

paragraphs.summary: Applicant cites Turkish article on Hamas recruitment; court finds recruitment described as voluntary, not forced.

propositions.text: Response to Information Request does not confirm Hamas forced recruitment; indicates limited info and Israeli forces engage in forced recruitment of collaborators.
propositions.quote: the Response to Information Request document dated July 31, 2013 does not confirm that Hamas engages in forced recruitment

propositions.text: Applicant does not fit collaborator profile targeted by Hamas or Fatah for harsh repercussions.
propositions.quote: Applicant, as a returnee to Palestine after having lived in the United States for two decades, does not fit the “collaborator” profile

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no confirmation of Hamas forced recruitment; Applicant does not fit collaborator profile targeted by Hamas or Fatah.

propositions.text: Applicant submits lack of PIF narrative details was determinative; would have added fears of forced recruitment if allowed to rewrite.
propositions.quote: Applicant maintains that had he been given the opportunity to re-write his narrative, he would have included details such as fears based on his attempted recruitment by Hamas and Fatah

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues lack of PIF details was determinative and would have added fears of forced recruitment if allowed to rewrite.

propositions.text: No evidence remedies lack of documentary corroboration; adverse credibility findings supported by implausible narrative.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence in the documentation the Applicant provided to the Court that would remedy the decision-maker’s finding

propositions.text: No reasonable probability that alleged incompetence would have changed original hearing result.
propositions.quote: There is no reasonable probability, in the case at bar, that but for the alleged incompetence, the original hearing would have yielded a different result

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence remedies lack of corroboration; no reasonable probability incompetence changed hearing result.

propositions.text: Application dismissed and no question certified for appeal.
propositions.quote: this application is dismissed and no question is certified for appeal

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application and refuses to certify any question for appeal.
